passage:
The Class 5 homework for Thursday was the same for everyone: some sums, a paragraph in Hindi, a drawing and a chapter to read.

Nandini wrote the three written jobs on a slip and guessed the time beside each: ten, twenty, thirty minutes. Adding them up, she smiled. One hour. That was all.

Anirban wound the kitchen timer to twenty minutes, worked until it rang, then drank water and stretched for five. The second block felt lighter, and the last page was finished before dinner.

Meher went straight to the drawing because colouring felt nice, then copied out her spelling list. By eight o'clock only the sums were left. Her eyes were heavy, and she raced through them and got three wrong.

Pranav had planned to start after dinner. Halfway through his tea he remembered his cousin was coming at six. He took a pencil to the plan, shifted the sums ahead of dinner, and kept the chapter for once the visitors had gone. When he closed his bag, nothing was left undone.

qa.q: How many minutes was the kitchen timer wound to?
qa.a: The kitchen timer was wound to twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Meher end up with mistakes while Pranav got everything done?
qa.a: Meher did the nice parts first and left the hard sums for when she was sleepy at eight o'clock, whereas Pranav noticed the six o'clock visit and shifted the sums ahead of dinner.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling after adding up the times?
qa.a: Relief and calm, since her smile shows the work now seemed small enough to manage.

qa.q: What could Meher try tomorrow to avoid rushing?
qa.a: Meher could start with the hard sums while she is fresh and keep the drawing as a treat for later.

grounding: Four approaches to finishing homework on time: listing and estimating, short timed blocks, easy parts first, and redoing the plan when the evening changes.
